title: Vintage Dates Versus Age Statements | Craft Beer School
desc: How a vintage year on a whisky label differs from an age statement, why whisky does not age in bottle like wine and how to work out the real age.
teaser: A 1998 vintage whisky is not 28 years old. To know its age you need a second date.
standfirst: Whisky labels carry two kinds of number that look similar but mean different things. An age statement tells you how long the whisky spent in a cask. A vintage tells you the year it was distilled. Mixing them up is easy and it can cost you money.
sections: An age statement counts years in the cask

An age statement, such as 12 years old, counts the time the youngest whisky in the bottle spent maturing in oak. It stops counting the day the whisky leaves the cask. A 12 year old bottled in 2010 is still a 12 year old today. Our guide to whisky age statements covers the rules in detail.

That is the key difference from wine. Wine can keep developing in a sealed bottle because it is low in alcohol and has a cork that lets in tiny amounts of air over years. Whisky at 40% ABV or more barely changes once it is in glass. Its maturation happened in the cask.
A vintage is the year of distillation

A vintage on a whisky label is the year the spirit was distilled and put into cask. A bottle marked 1998 tells you that much and nothing more on its own. It could have been bottled in 2008 after ten years in oak or in 2023 after twenty five.

That is why a vintage needs a second date. Responsible producers print the bottling year next to the vintage, for example distilled 1998, bottled 2016. Subtract one from the other and you have the age: 18 years. Scotch labelling rules expect a vintage to come with either a bottling year or an age statement for exactly this reason.

Vintage whiskies are usually single cask or small batch releases. Instead of blending many casks to a consistent house style, the producer bottles casks from one year and lets them show their own character. Two vintages of the same distillery can taste very different.

Vintages appeal to collectors and to people marking a birth year or anniversary. For the drinker, they offer a snapshot: what that distillery's spirit and that batch of casks became after a set time.
The vintage trap for wine drinkers

A wine lover sees 1998 and thinks of a mature wine that has developed for 28 years. With whisky, that thinking leads you astray. A 1998 vintage bottled in 2008 is a ten year old whisky that has sat in glass ever since. It has not become a 28 year old.

This matters when prices are high. Before paying a premium for an old vintage date, find the bottling year. If it is missing, ask. If nobody knows, treat the age as unknown and price it that way.

Years in cask also mean different things in different climates. In a cool Scottish warehouse, 18 years can bring slow, gentle oak influence. In India, where warehouses can run well above 30 °C in summer, spirit moves into and out of the wood faster and evaporation losses are much higher. Our guide to temperature swings in Indian warehouses explains why.

So an 8 year old Indian single malt and an 18 year old Scotch can show comparable oak character. Neither the vintage nor the age statement tells you how a whisky tastes. They tell you how long it spent in wood. Where it sat matters as much as how long.
Keeping a vintage bottle once you own it

Because whisky does not improve in glass, there is no reason to hold a vintage bottle for the sake of the whisky. Some people keep them as a record of a year that matters to them. That is a fine reason.

If you do keep one, store it upright, away from light and heat, in its box if it came with one. Check the fill level every year or two. A falling level is a sign the cork is letting spirit escape and the bottle should be opened before it loses more. Once opened, the air in a half empty bottle slowly flattens the aroma over months, so share it rather than nursing it for years.
Reading a vintage label step by step

• Find the distillation year. This is the vintage.
  • Find the bottling year, often printed on the back label or the neck.
  • Subtract to get years in cask.
  • Look for a cask number and type, such as refill hogshead or first fill sherry butt. That tells you the likely flavour direction.
  • Check the strength. Single cask vintages are often bottled at cask strength.

A label with a vintage, a bottling year, a cask number and an ABV gives you more information than most age statement bottles do. Learning to connect that information to what you smell is the skill that turns a label into a prediction you can test.

Look at the oldest bottle you own or have seen on a shop shelf. Find both dates or the age. Work out exactly how long it spent in oak. Then write down what you would expect it to taste like from the cask type before you open or taste it. Checking that guess is how you learn.
faqs: What does a vintage year mean on whisky?
It is the year the whisky was distilled. On its own it does not tell you the age, so look for a bottling year as well.
Does whisky get older in the bottle?
No. Maturation stops when whisky leaves the cask, so a sealed bottle stays the age it was when bottled.
How do I work out the age of a vintage whisky?
Subtract the distillation year from the bottling year. A whisky distilled in 1998 and bottled in 2016 is 18 years old.
